title: AI Changes the Learner. But Do We Know How?
author: Austin, Tina et al.
summary: Two educators, UCLA researcher Tina Austin and newsletter author 'Sam,' publicly work through a disagreement about whether AI changes learners' judgment, and the disagreement itself becomes a model for the classroom exercise they end up recommending. Sam's original claim was that AI-mediated decision-making displaces human judgment through mechanisms like distance and scapegoating, drawn from a small interview study of high-stakes professionals; Austin pushes back that the underlying study shows plausible mechanisms, not durable measured change, and that Sam's own remedy (having AI argue against itself) can let students merely watch an AI perform critical thinking rather than do it themselves. The piece is structured as an actual back-and-forth, including Sam conceding he stated inference as finding, before converging on a shared classroom protocol: students commit to a position before AI is introduced, then use AI as an opponent, then must construct and explain the counter-case themselves. It closes by acknowledging the central empirical question — whether repeated AI use durably changes learners' judgment — remains genuinely unanswered and requires longitudinal research neither author has yet completed.
points: A study showing plausible mechanisms of AI-induced judgment displacement is not the same as evidence that judgment durably changed — mind the gap between hypothesis and finding.
Having AI 'argue against itself' can produce a student who has only watched an impressive debate, not one who practiced the reasoning.
The fix isn't banning AI-mediated argument but sequencing it: fix a position before AI enters, then make the student construct (not just judge) the opposing case.
A practical 40-minute classroom protocol: 10 minutes silent baseline, 15 minutes with AI building the counter-case, 15 minutes comparing divergent answers aloud.
Teachers should share their own baseline position alongside students' — modeling the same discipline they're asking for.
quotes: I was writing about a study in AI and Ethics that interviewed twenty-two professionals in healthcare and the military, people for whom a bad call is a catastrophe rather than an inconvenience. The researchers describe something they call trait displacement, and they name five drivers: distance, abstraction, perceived inferiority, the added entity, and scapegoating.
A screen puts a layer between you and the thing you are deciding about. The person becomes a percentage. The more often the machine is right, the less you argue with it.

Asking AI to argue with itself does not automatically protect human judgement. If the model supplies the answer, the objection, and the rebuttal, the learner can remain a spectator throughout an impressive simulation of critical thinking.

Twenty-two interviews can surface mechanisms that people recognise and describe. They cannot show that anyone's judgement durably changed. I called it evidence of a change when what I had was a well-described hypothesis about one.

On the 'learner as spectator' point, this is what I mean: a student can ask AI for an answer, ask it to challenge that answer, and then ask which argument is stronger. The transcript contains all the features we associate with critical thinking: claims, counterclaims, evidence, and revision, but they were generated by the model.

Give every student the same question. Have them fix their own position before any model sees it. That baseline does not have to be written: for some students writing is not the accessible route, and what matters is that the position exists and is recorded somehow, spoken, drawn or typed.
